findings.title: Point the build at an actual installer
findings.whyItBreaks: example.com is a reserved example domain, and the repository contains no installer at this URL. curl lacks --fail, so an HTTP error response is still piped to sh; the shell rejects that response and the Docker build fails.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Each image build executes the current contents of a remote script as root. If the origin or its content is compromised or changed, the build can run arbitrary code and produce a compromised image; this line pins neither the script nor its integrity.

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: The shell reports the status of the last pipeline command, sh. If curl fails and supplies no input, sh exits successfully, so Docker can continue building an image without running the installer.

findings.title: Propagate installer download failures
findings.whyItBreaks: If curl fails before producing output, sh receives empty input and exits 0. The pipeline reports success, so the Docker build can proceed without the installer having run.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key signal in the exported helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing when the key is absent, but this helper discards it and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish an absent key from a key explicitly storing an empty string.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Run now returns after launching goroutines, without waiting for their sends. A caller that closes results after Run returns can race with a pending send and panic; output order can also differ from the input order.

findings.title: Wait for workers before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Run now returns after launching the goroutines, without waiting for their sends. A caller that treats Run's return as completion can observe missing results; before this change, every send completed before Run returned.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: Run now returns after launching the goroutines, without waiting for their sends. A caller that closes results after Run returns can race with these sends and trigger a send-on-closed-channel panic; callers also can no longer rely on Run returning after all results have been sent.

findings.title: Require admin status and a matching tenant to authorize deletion

findings.title: Preserve tenant and admin checks when authorizing deletion

findings.title: Preserve parse failures for callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts JSON syntax and field validation errors into valid-looking defaults. updateFontSize then changes the font size and calls save, so invalid stored data can be overwritten and callers cannot distinguish a parse failure from legitimate settings.

findings.whyItBreaks: For input such as {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"large"}, parseSettings now returns the light defaults. updateFontSize then saves those defaults with the new font size, discarding the existing dark theme. Previously, the validation error propagated and save was not called.

findings.title: Restore the positive limit slice

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window

findings.title: Return cached values only before the TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: With a positive TTL, a fresh entry fails this condition and is deleted, so get returns null. Once the entry is older than the TTL, the condition succeeds and get returns it without deleting it, so expired values remain available indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove every completed job while pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forEach shifts the array while the index advances. For [done, done], removing the first item shifts the second into index 0, then forEach advances to index 1 and leaves that completed job in the result.

findings.title: Return cached values only while they are unexpired
findings.whyItBreaks: For a positive TTL, a fresh entry has an age below ttlMs, so this condition fails and get deletes it. Once the entry is older than ttlMs, the condition succeeds and get returns the expired value. This reverses cache-hit and expiration behavior.

findings.title: Remove adjacent completed jobs during pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forward forEach shifts the next job into the current index, then forEach advances past it. For example, [done, done, pending] leaves one completed job in the returned queue.

findings.title: Restore the live-entry TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: With a positive TTL, a fresh entry has age below the TTL, so this condition fails and get() deletes it and returns null. Once the entry is older than the TTL, the condition succeeds and get() returns the expired value.

findings.title: Prune done jobs without splicing during iteration
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing a completed job shifts later jobs while forEach continues using the original indexes. For two adjacent completed jobs, removing the first shifts the second to index 0; the next callback visits index 1, so the second completed job remains in the returned queue. This also mutates the caller's input array, unlike the previous filter-based implementation.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input result

findings.title: Avoid reordering the caller's rows

findings.title: Preserve the caller's row order in busiest

findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator sorts numbers lexicographically. For scores 2, 10, and 100, reversing the result gives [2, 100, 10]; with n=2, the cutoff becomes 100, so topPlayers returns only the player scoring 100 and omits the player scoring 10.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers lexicographically. With input scores [2, 10], sorting and reversing produces [2, 10]; for n=1 the cutoff is 2, and filtering then slicing can return the score-2 player instead of the score-10 player.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before selecting the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: JavaScript's default sort compares values as strings. With scores [2, 10], sort then reverse produces [2, 10], so topPlayers(players, 1) can choose a cutoff of 2 and return the 2-point player.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can stop at the first differing character, exposing how much of an attacker-supplied signature matches through timing. The result gates processor execution at app/webhook.py:14, so repeated probes can help an attacker forge an accepted signature.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: String equality can return early based on the first differing character, exposing matching signature prefixes through timing. Repeated measurements can help an attacker forge a signature; handle() accepts a verified signature before calling processor().

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison for webhook signatures
findings.whyItBreaks: Python string equality can take different time depending on how many leading characters match. At `handle`'s authorization gate, repeated submissions can expose the matching prefix of the expected HMAC, enabling timing-based signature recovery and forged webhook requests.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits after recording the ledger entry, then balance updates run outside it. If either update fails, the ledger can persist without matching balance changes; if the second update fails, only one account may be changed.

findings.title: Keep the balance updates inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction exits after inserting the ledger row at line 23, then this line applies the balance changes outside it. If either UPDATE fails, the ledger entry remains committed; if the credit update fails after the debit succeeds, the accounts are also left imbalanced.

findings.title: Keep both balance updates in the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the transaction block exits, but the balance updates run afterward. If either update fails, the ledger remains committed with unchanged or partially changed balances; the transfer is no longer atomic.

findings.title: Keep billing dates independent of the host timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The helper changed from UTC getters to host-local getters. The same instant, such as 2024-01-01T00:30:00Z, now produces 2023-12-31 in a US Pacific runtime and 2024-01-01 in UTC, so billing-day results vary by deployment timezone.

findings.title: Keep billing-day results independent of the host timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The local getters make the billing date depend on the runtime timezone. For example, 2025-01-01T00:30:00Z formats as 2024-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles, whereas the previous UTC implementation returned 2025-01-01. sameBillingDay inherits this change, so timestamps on the same UTC date can compare as different billing days.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The new local-date getters can assign an instant to a different billing day depending on the server timezone. For example, 2024-01-01T00:30:00Z is December 31 in America/Los_Angeles, so billingDay returns a different date than before; sameBillingDay inherits that change.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: If two tenants use the same account ID, the first read caches its profile under that account ID. A read for the other tenant then returns the first tenant's profile without calling its fetcher, giving the caller the wrong tenant, account, and display name.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level cache is shared across calls. After reading account X for tenant A, a read of account X for tenant B hits the same key and returns tenant A’s profile without calling fetchProfile for tenant B.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level cache is now keyed only by account. After a request for an account in one tenant is cached, a request for the same account in another tenant returns the first tenant’s Profile at line 15 and skips fetching the second tenant’s profile at line 16. The returned tenant and displayName can therefore belong to the wrong tenant.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw an error; it now returns "", which is also a valid stored value. Callers cannot tell missing data from an intentionally empty value. `loadAll` now returns that fallback in its array instead of propagating the missing-key error.

findings.title: Propagate missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key used to throw, but the catch now returns an empty string. Callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a key whose stored value is empty; loadAll also returns that fallback instead of propagating the error.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw `missing: <key>`; the catch now returns `""`, which callers cannot distinguish from a stored empty string. `loadAll` therefore returns an array containing an empty string where it previously propagated the error.

findings.title: Keep retry's timeoutMs input working
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing callers pass { maxAttempts, timeoutMs }. With the new Config, they lack the required retries field and provide no timeout value. At runtime, retry reads undefined at line 8, making deadline NaN; the guard at line 10 then always passes, so the configured timeout is disabled.

findings.title: Rethrow the final retryBackground error
findings.whyItBreaks: If every callback invocation throws, the catch continues through the loop and retryBackground returns normally. Callers receive the same void result as a successful invocation and cannot detect that all attempts failed.

findings.title: Preserve the existing retry timeout configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and retry previously accepted { maxAttempts, timeoutMs }. The new interface removes timeoutMs and requires retries and timeout, breaking existing TypeScript consumers. At runtime, an existing JavaScript caller has config.timeout === undefined: line 8 computes a NaN deadline, and the guard at line 10 never stops retries, so the configured timeout is ignored.

findings.title: Count retries after the initial background call
findings.whyItBreaks: The public config field retries describes additional calls after the initial attempt, but the loop uses it as the total number of calls. With retries=1, a failing callback runs once and is never retried; with retries=0, it is never called.

findings.title: Expose failure when background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: When every callback invocation throws, the catch continues until the loop ends and retryBackground returns normally with void. Because the function is exported, callers cannot distinguish exhausted failure from success.

findings.title: Preserve the existing timeout config for retry callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Config was exported with maxAttempts and timeoutMs; it now requires retries and timeout. Existing TypeScript callers passing the old config no longer type-check. Existing JavaScript callers pass no timeout, so Date.now() + undefined becomes NaN and the deadline guard at line 10 never returns early.

findings.title: Count retries after the initial background attempt
findings.whyItBreaks: The public retries field is used as the total invocation limit. With retries: 1, a failing first invocation exhausts the loop, so the function performs zero retries.

findings.title: Expose the final background callback failure
findings.whyItBreaks: After every callback attempt throws, the catch continues and the function eventually returns void, indistinguishably from a successful call. The exported API gives callers no way to detect that the operation never succeeded.

findings.title: Compute the length of numeric values
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now permits numbers, but numeric values have no `length` property. A numeric input therefore produces `len=undefined` at runtime, and the union property access is invalid under TypeScript checking.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading their length
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed prop type accepts numbers, but numbers have no length property. Passing value={42} interpolates undefined and renders the input with defaultValue="len=undefined".

findings.title: Convert numeric values before reading their length
findings.whyItBreaks: `value` can now be a number, which has no `.length` property. TypeScript reports an error at line 6; if the code is emitted anyway, a numeric prop renders as `len=undefined`.

findings.title: Keep an explicit buffer limit for Git output
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores Node's 1 MiB default. The Git diff at line 140 can exceed that size; spawnSync then reports a buffer error, and this call throws before the review handling block, so the PR review does not run.

findings.title: Preserve the larger buffer for Git output
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the 64 MiB maxBuffer makes spawnSync use its 1 MiB default. The git diff call at line 140 captures the full patch, so a diff larger than 1 MiB fails before review(bundle) runs and the review workflow aborts.

findings.title: Preserve the large-diff output limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer leaves spawnSync at its 1 MiB default. The full patch is captured through this helper at line 140, so a diff exceeding that limit makes the Git command fail and aborts the review.

findings.title: Restore the read-only Codex sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the CLI override lets Codex use its configured sandbox mode. With `workspace-write`, Codex can edit the workspace; this function sets its working directory to `opts.repoPath` (line 24), so a review run can modify the checkout. Codex documents the configuration precedence and sandbox modes [here](https://developers.openai.com/codex/config-basic) and [here](https://developers.openai.com/codex/sandboxing).

findings.title: Keep Codex review runs in read-only mode
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` makes the sandbox depend on Codex's configured permissions. With the `workspace-write` mode, Codex can edit the workspace and run routine local commands; here `opts.repoPath` is its working directory at line 24. Untrusted repository content can therefore steer a review run into modifying the checkout. Codex documents that permission defaults are configurable and that `workspace-write` permits workspace edits ([sandbox documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/sandboxing)).

findings.title: Keep Codex execution read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: The wrapper runs Codex with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 24), but no longer pins its sandbox to read-only. Codex can inherit a `workspace-write` setting, which permits editing workspace files ([Codex sandbox docs](https://developers.openai.com/codex/sandboxing)); a review prompt can therefore modify the repository being reviewed.

findings.title: Anchor inline-comment lines to the posted PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checked-out HEAD, these lines build the patch and changed-file set from HEAD, but postReview submits comments with commit_id=headSha. If the merge checkout includes base-side changes that shift lines in a PR-changed file, findings' RIGHT-side line numbers refer to a different file version than the posted review. GitHub can reject those inline comments; the existing fallback then posts only the review body, dropping all inline comments.

findings.title: Diff against the PR head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checkout's HEAD, these lines build the patch and changed-file set from baseSha..HEAD, while the bundle still identifies PR_HEAD_SHA and the review is posted against it at line 178. The result can review one commit and attach that verdict to another.

findings.title: Keep the diff anchored at the PR merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA points to a base branch tip that advanced after the PR branch forked, diffing that tip directly against HEAD includes base-only changes in the patch and changed-file set. The review can then analyze files and changes that are not part of the PR.

findings.title: Preserve inserted prompt text literally
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace treats replacement strings containing tokens such as $& and $' specially. A patch containing those tokens is therefore altered in the serialized bundle and again when inserted into the critic prompt, so Codex may review different content from the actual patch. The previous callback replacements inserted these values literally.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences in inserted prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets replacement tokens in bundle.patch: for example, $& inserts the matched {{PATCH}} marker, $$ loses a dollar sign, and $' inserts the critic prompt suffix. A diff containing these sequences reaches the critic altered, which can cause it to review incorrect patch content. The same regression affects the bundle and findings insertions on lines 25 and 32.

findings.title: Preserve literal prompt replacement text
findings.whyItBreaks: Passing bundle.patch as a replacement string makes String.replace interpret sequences such as $&, $$, $` and $' instead of preserving them literally. A diff containing one of these sequences is altered in the critic prompt; the same issue affects the bundle and findings substitutions on lines 25 and 32. The critic can therefore review content different from the actual diff.

findings.title: Keep the reviewed commit SHA in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: If the initial review request fails and the PR advances before the fallback runs, this request omits commit_id. GitHub then associates the review event and verdict with the PR's most recent commit, even though runGithub analyzed headSha. A REQUEST_CHANGES verdict can therefore appear to apply to code this run did not review.

findings.title: Keep fallback reviews pinned to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: If the first review request fails and the PR head advances before the fallback runs, this request omits commit_id. GitHub then associates the review with the PR's latest commit, even though runGithub passes the earlier headSha to postReview. A changes-requested verdict can therefore apply to a commit the review did not analyze.

findings.title: Pin the fallback review to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The fallback no longer sends the captured headSha. GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the PR's most recent commit, so if the PR advances after analysis and the first POST fails, the fallback can apply a stale REQUEST_CHANGES review to the new commit. The check run remains tied to the captured headSha at line 184.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating them
findings.whyItBreaks: An invalid severity now becomes P1, and missing required fields become empty strings or zero. For example, normalizeFinding({severity: "BAD"}) returns a Finding-shaped value instead of reporting malformed input; normalizeReview then includes that value in its findings array. Callers cannot distinguish malformed input from a real finding.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict option on normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function no longer accepts its second strict argument. Typed consumers calling normalizeReview(raw, false) will fail to compile; JavaScript consumers lose the former tolerant behavior, which filtered malformed findings.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: For an object such as `{}`, normalizeFinding now returns a Finding with severity P1, category bug, title Untitled finding, empty file and explanation, and line 0. Previously, missing required fields and invalid severity or category threw; normalizeReview either propagated that error in strict mode or filtered the item in non-strict mode. Callers of these exported functions now receive a fabricated finding and cannot distinguish malformed input from a real result.

findings.title: Preserve strict validation for malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: An invalid severity becomes P1, an invalid category becomes bug, and omitted required fields become empty strings or 0. normalizeReview then returns these entries through its map at line 131, so callers cannot distinguish malformed output from a real finding. Previously normalizeFinding threw for invalid fields, strict mode propagated that error, and lenient mode dropped the entry. Removing normalizeReview's exported strict argument also breaks TypeScript callers that pass false.

findings.title: Keep repository selection explicit for manual dispatch lookups
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before actions/checkout and without GH_REPO or -R. On a clean runner, gh cannot infer the repository. The command substitutions then write empty head/base outputs, which checkout consumes at line 45 and the review CLI receives at lines 56–57; the requested PR may not be reviewed.

findings.title: Keep the explicit repository when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before the checkout step. The workflow no longer supplies REPO, and gh pr view relies on a local repository or GH_REPO when -R is omitted. In a clean runner workspace, it cannot identify the repository and ref resolution fails. See the [gh pr view manual](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_view) and [gh environment manual](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_help_environment).

findings.title: Keep explicit repository context for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so these commands run before the workflow's first checkout at line 43. Without -R or GH_REPO, gh pr view must infer a repository from the current directory; a clean runner workspace has no Git remote to infer, so ref resolution fails and the review never starts.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null or an object missing required fields previously threw a malformed-review error. They now return a RawReview with empty or coerced fields, so callers cannot distinguish invalid review output from a legitimate empty review.

findings.title: Reject malformed review payloads instead of returning an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, non-objects and missing or wrongly typed required fields threw an error. Now inputs such as `{}` produce a RawReview with an empty summary and empty arrays. A caller can no longer distinguish malformed review output from a legitimate review with no findings, and may treat an incomplete review as a pass. The function is exported, so this broken contract applies even though this snapshot has no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Keep rejecting malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, malformed input or missing/wrong-typed required fields threw an error. These defaults now return a RawReview with empty fields, so callers of this exported function can mistake invalid review output for a valid review with no findings.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR refs during manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: A workflow_dispatch event has a pr_number input but no pull_request object. The checkout therefore falls back to github.ref, and PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are empty. The next step still invokes the reviewer with the requested PR number, so manual reviews run from the workflow branch without the requested PR's resolved refs. The previous workflow resolved the head and base from that PR number.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR before checkout on manual runs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, pull_request.head.sha is empty, so checkout uses github.ref—the branch selected for the workflow run. The requested PR number is only passed to the CLI later, so the workflow runs the self-review tool from the dispatch branch rather than the requested PR head. The removed Resolve PR refs step previously checked out that PR's head.

findings.title: Resolve the selected PR before checking out on manual runs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, pull_request.head.sha is absent, so checkout falls back to github.ref, the ref selected for the workflow run. That ref is independent of the PR number input. The previous workflow resolved the selected PR's head before checkout, and the workflow comment says the checked-out PR source is the review tool. Manual runs can therefore execute a different revision than the requested PR; PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are also empty on that event.

findings.title: Preserve the Git output buffer for large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit 64 MiB cap makes `spawnSync` use its 1 MiB default. When `git diff` at line 100 produces more than 1 MiB on stdout, Node terminates the child and truncates its output; `git()` then throws at line 12, so the local review never receives the patch. [Node.js documents the default and cap behavior](https://nodejs.org/download/release/v22.18.0/docs/api/child_process.html).

findings.title: Keep the larger buffer for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal captures the full `git diff` output at src/adapters/local.ts:100. With maxBuffer omitted, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default; a larger patch makes the subprocess fail, and the status check at line 12 throws instead of reviewing it. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these diffs.

findings.title: Keep the larger Git output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: runLocal captures the full `git diff` output through this helper at line 100. Without an explicit maxBuffer, Node allows 1 MiB on stdout; for a larger diff it terminates Git and truncates the output, then this helper throws, so the review never runs.

findings.title: Keep review failures blocking in the Needlefish check
findings.whyItBreaks: When review or review posting throws, this publishes the Needlefish check with conclusion `neutral`. GitHub treats neutral required checks as successful, so a branch protected by this check can allow a PR through even though the check summary says the review failed.

findings.title: Keep review errors as failing checks
findings.whyItBreaks: When review(bundle) throws, this posts the completed Needlefish check with conclusion neutral. A neutral conclusion can satisfy a required status check, so the PR may be mergeable even though the check says the review failed and did not pass.

findings.title: Keep the diff and changed-file set on the same PR revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch now comes from the current remote PR, while changedFileSet still runs git diff against the local checkout's HEAD (lines 57 and 144). If the PR advances after the workflow checkout, the bundle combines revisions; findings for files added in the newer diff are then dropped by inlineComments' changedPaths filter at line 70.

findings.title: Keep review errors as a failing check
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path changed the Needlefish check conclusion from failure to neutral. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required status, so a repository requiring this check can allow a merge after the review errored. The error remains in the check summary and process.exitCode is still 1, but neither changes this check run's neutral conclusion. [GitHub required status check guidance](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/troubleshooting-required-status-checks)

findings.title: Keep manual reviews from executing PR-controlled code
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow_dispatch path bypasses the same-repository condition at line 24 and checks out the requested PR head. This command runs that checkout's src/cli.ts with GH_TOKEN available; the workflow grants pull-requests: write and checks: write. A manually reviewed fork PR can therefore run code with those permissions on the self-hosted runner. The previous workflow ran the trusted main checkout as the tool.

findings.title: Provide the reviewer files in the checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: This commit tracks only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, or src/cli.ts. The new install runs in the repository root and the next step invokes the absent src/cli.ts, so the review workflow cannot complete from this checkout. Previously, the install and CLI came from the separate frankekn/needlefish checkout.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted ref
findings.whyItBreaks: The checkout is the PR head, so a PR can change src/cli.ts and have that version run as the reviewer. It can suppress findings or misuse the GH_TOKEN supplied to the step, which has pull-requests:write and checks:write permissions. The review result is therefore controlled by the code being reviewed.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Run the reviewer from a trusted revision
findings.whyItBreaks: This command runs src/cli.ts from the PR-head checkout. A PR changing the reviewer can make it report no findings or skip review, causing the workflow to present a clean result for code it controls. The same step supplies a write-capable GITHUB_TOKEN at line 56.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Preserve valid severity variants when normalizing findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts runtime input as any and maps each finding through normalizeFinding. A severity such as " p1 " was previously trimmed and uppercased to P1; the exact membership check now rejects it and returns P3. Consumers therefore receive a valid P1 finding classified as the lowest severity.

findings.title: Preserve case normalization for severity values
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts unvalidated input and maps its findings through normalizeFinding at line 132. A severity such as "p0" or " P1 " previously normalized to P0 or P1; the exact-value check now maps it to P3, so the returned review loses the finding's intended urgency.

findings.title: Preserve case normalization for valid severities
findings.whyItBreaks: A raw severity of " p0 " previously normalized to P0. The exact-match check now rejects it and returns P3, so normalizeReview can return a critical finding as the lowest severity.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: With `env` omitted, `spawnSync` inherits `process.env`, including any GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or GITHUB_API_TOKEN. A prompt influenced by untrusted repository content can lead Codex to read and return those credentials; read-only mode does not prevent reading environment variables.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex child environment
findings.whyItBreaks: With `env` omitted, `spawnSync` inherits `process.env`, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The Codex process and its child commands can then access those credentials; the previous code explicitly removed them.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting `env` makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN` that this code previously removed. Codex can run commands while reviewing repository content, so prompt-injected content can cause a command to read these credentials and expose them through its output.

findings.title: Keep fork pull requests off the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the same-repository condition lets fork pull requests reach this job. It checks out the PR head, runs pnpm install, then executes the checked-out src/cli.ts, so a contributor can run arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner and potentially compromise its host or other jobs.

findings.title: Keep fork PR code off the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted condition restricted this job to same-repository PRs. Now a fork PR can reach the workflow, which checks out its head at line 23, installs dependencies, and executes the PR-controlled CLI at line 34 on a self-hosted runner. That gives untrusted code access to the runner's host environment.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard for this self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed condition was the job's only fork exclusion. When repository settings allow a fork pull_request workflow to run, its PR head is checked out at line 23, dependencies are installed at line 28, and PR-controlled src/cli.ts is executed at line 34 on the self-hosted runner. Untrusted code can compromise that runner and access its ambient credentials. GitHub warns that fork PR code can compromise self-hosted runners and potentially access secrets or the GITHUB_TOKEN ([GitHub secure use reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use)).

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner cleanup durations
findings.whyItBreaks: With NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0, the previous guard returned 0, so the timeout handler escalated to SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM. This guard now rejects 0 and substitutes the 5000 ms default at line 5, delaying escalation by five seconds. NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 likewise now uses its 2000 ms default instead of allowing immediate completion after SIGKILL.

findings.title: Preserve zero-delay runner overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: With either timing environment variable set to `0`, this change substitutes the default: the SIGKILL grace period becomes 5000 ms instead of 0, or the post-SIGKILL give-up wait becomes 2000 ms instead of 0. That silently defeats an explicit setting to escalate or return immediately.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner delay settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous check accepted 0, which Node passes to setTimeout as an immediate delay. Now setting NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 silently imposes the 5000 ms fallback before SIGKILL, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 silently imposes the 2000 ms fallback before giving up waiting. This prevents users relying on either zero-delay setting from getting the configured behavior.

findings.title: Keep uncovered changed files in the deep review
findings.whyItBreaks: For a large bundle whose map pass returns more than six hotspots with distinct files, this slice excludes hotspot seven onward. The removed coverage backstop no longer adds those files to a deep pass, so findings in them can be missed.

findings.title: Restore the coverage backstop for unmapped files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews keep only the six highest-risk hotspots. With the coverage backstop removed, any changed file omitted from those hotspots is never deep-reviewed and produces no residual risk, so the review can miss defects in that file.

findings.title: Forward deep-pass residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass can return unresolved or blocking residual risks, but this line replaces them with an empty list before the critic call. The critic therefore cannot account for those specific risks, and they cannot reach the final verdict through the prior aggregation path.

findings.title: Preserve coverage for changed files outside the six selected hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: The six-hotspot slice can exclude changed files that the map pass did not place in a selected hotspot. The removed coverage backstop used to add those files to a deep-review pass; now they receive no deep review and are absent from the final candidate.

findings.title: Keep distinct same-title findings separate during deduplication
findings.whyItBreaks: Findings with the same file, start line, category, and normalized first 60 title characters now share a key even when their whyItBreaks details differ. The map keeps only one, dropping a distinct finding from the large-review result.

findings.title: Keep the requested focus in large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: For a large bundle with a non-null focus, the deep prompt is no longer populated from bundle.focus. The review model therefore loses the caller’s requested emphasis, so it can omit the targeted checks that the previous path supplied.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute count
findings.whyItBreaks: For 59,600 ms, this computes 0 minutes and 60 seconds, displaying `60s` instead of `1m 0s`. For 119,600 ms, it displays `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. The rendered call and total durations can therefore be malformed near minute boundaries.

findings.title: Normalize seconds after rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: Rounding the seconds remainder independently can produce non-normalized output. For example, 59,999 ms renders as "60s" and 119,999 ms as "1m 60s", instead of "1m 0s" and "2m 0s".

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: When the remaining milliseconds round to 60 seconds, minutes still come from the unrounded duration. For example, 59,500 ms renders as `60s` instead of `1m 0s`, and 119,500 ms renders as `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. These values appear in the Markdown stats.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guard lets parsePositiveInteger("0", ...) return 0, even though the exported function name and its error message promise a positive integer. Callers receive a value that violates the parser's public contract.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported parsePositiveInteger function promises a positive integer, but this check accepts 0. Since Number("") is also 0, empty input is accepted as well, so callers can receive a value that violates the parser's contract.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guard accepts zero, so parsePositiveInteger("0", label) returns 0 at line 35 despite the exported function and its error text promising a positive integer.
